items.title: Generation speed at full load (4.42 M)
items.text: On the fair test (v3.2), the full node passes 15 of 15 minutes at 3.33 M per GPU and 14 of 15 at 3.72 M. At full load (4.4 M per GPU), generation speed is the limit: in the failing minutes each GPU runs 15 to 20 requests with 0.9 to 1.6 M context tokens, and a generation step takes about 88 ms. Four changes on Oct 2 raised generation speed at full load: prompt chunks sized by their cost (+2.7 tok/s), decode-after-prefill off (+2.7 tok/s), the FA4 kernel for the draft model (+4.65 tok/s) and a faster index-score kernel (+3.6 tok/s). Next: a faster top-k and a faster index score for generation steps.

items.title: Median first token: passes (rule now under 3 s)
items.text: Fixed Oct 1 20:41. M3.1 is an image-capable model, so the engine tokenised every conversation, turned the tokens back into text and tokenised it all again; our caches only sped up the first pass. Passing the cached tokens straight through (identical tokens on 300/300 real prompts) plus one cache shared by the 8 tokenizer processes cut the median first token at 2.23 M from 0.85 s to 0.54 s; every minute is now 0.49–0.61 s against the 1 s limit. Per request (median): tokenising 0.045 s, hand-off 0.04 s, waiting 0.003 s, prompt processing 0.22 s, first visible word back to the client 0.10 s.

items.title: Slowest 1% of first tokens: fixed at 2.23 M (no longer an SLA rule)
items.text: Dropped from the SLA on Oct 1, and fixed anyway: a 300k+ token uncached prompt ran 16k-token pieces back to back for 20+ s while its engine generated nothing. One decode step after each piece (Oct 1 21:24) brought the slowest 1% at 2.23 M to 8.2 s, better than production's 10.4 s on the same requests, with every minute at or under 14.5 s.

items.title: Prompts processed again at full load
items.text: At 4.42 M we re-process 2.75× as many uncached prompt tokens as production: 84% of the extra comes from conversations whose cached prompt was evicted between turns (the largest share after 2–10 minutes idle). More cache memory (0.76, adopted Oct 1 05:52) cut those evictions.

items.title: Errors: one client's tool schemas (Oct 3)
items.text: On another node's sessions (buckets b02+b03), one session sent 218 tools per request, and 44 of them had "type": {}. Our engine rejected all 60 requests of that session with HTTP 400; production served them. The gateway now deletes only invalid type values (TOOL_SCHEMA_FIX_TYPE): the rerun had 0 errors and 14 of 15 minutes passed (was 1 of 15).

engineering.name: Faster sparse attention (generation steps and prompt chunks, bitwise equal)
engineering.text: generation steps: one tile per (request, KV head) for all 8 draft tokens, 6.0× faster bit for bit; twin +23.4 tok/s (+35%). Prompt chunks: a device-built work list (no host sync per layer), 1.8× faster bit for bit, 0 mismatches in 36,000 live calls; twin +4.05 tok/s. Both adopted
engineering.ref: twin v3_ab_sattnv2_cl_1x · PROGRESS.md Oct 3 11:34–13:34 · node kernels/sattn/

engineering.name: Faster index-score kernel for prompt chunks
engineering.text: a warp-specialized rewrite of the indexer's score kernel: bitwise equal, 3.9–5.0× faster on long prompt chunks (58–66% of FP8 peak vs 12.5%); GSM8K 96.74%; full-load twin: generation +3.62 tok/s, 12/15 vs 7/15 minutes
engineering.ref: twin v3_ab_isv2_cl_1x · PROGRESS.md Oct 2 21:34–23:25 · node kernels/idx/

engineering.name: Faster index score for generation steps (bitwise equal)
engineering.text: bit-exact, 1.85–2.3× faster on its own. First twin (Oct 3 06:33): no clear change while steps took ~90 ms; re-test on the newest stack (steps ~55 ms): generation +7.86 tok/s (CI +6.0..+10.0), 15/15 in both groups
engineering.ref: twins v3_ab_isvv2_cl_1x and v3_ab_isvv2b_cl_1x · PROGRESS.md Oct 3 06:33, 18:58

engineering.name: Faster top-k for the indexer (bitwise equal)
engineering.text: a threshold-filter top-k with an exact fallback for ties: bit-equal on GPU and on live traffic (38,400 calls, 0 mismatches); 6.8–10.1× on prompt chunks, 3.8–5.5× on generation steps; full-load twin: generation +2.94 tok/s, 12/15 vs 11/15 minutes
engineering.ref: twin v3_ab_tkv2_cl_1x · PROGRESS.md Oct 3 01:42–04:30 · node kernels/idx/topk_v2.py

engineering.name: FA4 attention for the draft model
engineering.text: production's draft attention backend; at full load generation +4.65 tok/s (95% CI +3.6..+5.9) with the same draft acceptance (3.60). It only pays since the draft replays its CUDA graph (Oct 2 00:12): before that, launch overhead hid the kernel time

engineering.name: Verify fewer draft tokens per request (DSpark ragged verify)
engineering.text: the fork's 'compact' mode cannot run on our stack: a boot guard stops it with DP attention and CUDA graphs, our attention path assumes 8 rows per request (wrong outputs), and DP padding keeps the MoE work at 8 rows per request. The verify width is only ~26% of a step, so an engine rewrite waits behind the indexer kernels

engineering.name: Fused verify kernels for 4-bit KV
engineering.text: production's in-house verify kernels let it keep 4-bit KV with speculative decoding and training-compatible numerics off; profile our verify step first (index, top-k, sparse attention shares) before writing our own

engineering.name: Attention over both GPUs (our own patch)
engineering.text: production runs attention split over the two GPUs of a worker (no lockstep); our training-compatible numerics force attention onto one GPU. A max-type index score can be merged across GPUs exactly, so our own patch could lift that guard (estimate +6–15% generation speed at 3.34 M; large effort, GSM8K check needed)

engineering.name: MiniMax's prompt-attention kernel (MSA)
engineering.text: now loadable in our image (a one-line gate fix compiles it; prebuilt objects link), but prompt attention is only ~11–23% of prompt time, so the expected gain at 3.34 M is +1–4 tok/s; a 15-minute GPU check for identical output comes first

engineering.name: Pair the two GPUs' prompt pieces (prefill delayer)
engineering.text: the built-in delayer holds a lone prompt piece up to 30 scheduling passes so both GPUs process prompts in the same step; with the draft-graph fix it lifted 3.34 M from 11/15 to 15/15 (generation 64.1 → 74.5 tok/s, median first token 0.65 → 1.45 s)

engineering.name: Draft model replays its CUDA graph
engineering.text: the draft captured CUDA graphs but never replayed them with DP attention on; the gate fix took 3.34 M from 2/15 to 11/15 and generation from 51.5 to 64.1 tok/s (production 64.8)

engineering.name: Tokenise each prompt once
engineering.text: for requests without images the engine passes our cached tokens through instead of decoding them to text and re-tokenising (identical tokens); with the shared cache, median first token at 2.23 M 0.85 → 0.54 s

engineering.name: Decode step after each prefill
engineering.text: after any prompt piece on either GPU the next step generates; at 2.23 M the slowest-1% first token fell to 8.2 s (production 10.4) and every minute passed the old strict rule for the first time; its effect at 3.34 M (generation speed) is queued

engineering.name: One tokenisation cache shared by an engine's tokenizer processes
engineering.text: each conversation's previous turn is reused whichever of the 8 processes gets the next one; 2.23 M: 12/15 with every minute inside the median rule (10 and 11 without it)

engineering.name: Per-request timing breakdown under load
engineering.text: engine timers (sampled every 30 s) put 0.7–1.0 s of the mean first token outside the GPU scheduler, even at low load; the shared-cache run at 2.23 M (started 19:10) logs per-request stamps that split it into tokenising, hand-off to the GPU scheduler and the return path

engineering.name: MiniMax's prompt-attention kernel inside our engine
engineering.text: identical output and 2.16 ms per call vs our 4.81 ms; the gather and scale steps add 1.5 ms (a fused gather could reach about 1.85×). Its toolchain (CuTe-DSL 4.5) and our engine image (4.6) cannot share one process

engineering.name: Faster prompt kernels of our own
engineering.text: autotune our Triton attention and indexer kernels on recorded prompt shapes, checked bit for bit against the current ones

engineering.name: Dynamo retest with per-GPU-half cache events
engineering.text: check that both GPUs' cache events reach the router, then rerun at half load

engineering.text: twin stopped: the engine's own binding (SYS_NICE) put group B's memory policy on NUMA nodes 0-1 (its GPUs are on nodes 2-3), so the kernel OOM killer stopped group-A engines 3 times during boot. Each engine fits on its own node (about 580 of 755 GB). Retest only with explicit per-engine pins (launcher CPUSET/MEMS) on all 4 engines; expected gain is small (+0.8 tok/s)

gap.note: On v3.1 requests our generation speed already beats production's at {load:best_0.5} M ({dec:best_0.5} vs {pdec:best_0.5} tok/s, Oct 1 {at:best_0.5}). The gap is prompt-processing speed, the two-GPU lockstep and per-request time outside GPU math. (This retires the older '75 vs 212 tok/s per stream' note, which current data contradicts.)

howto: TPM per GPU = tokens processed per minute (prompt including cached, plus output) ÷ 8 GPUs: the same formula as production's dashboard. Our loads come from production's request logs, which read about {ec_hub_ratio}× lower than production's engine counters.
Load we sent = the TPM per GPU that the replayed production requests ask for, not what we served. It rises by adding conversations, never by speeding up time.

Production has two numbers. {prod_full} M = production on exactly the requests our full-load replay sends; compare our runs with this. {ec_range} M = production's full load per GPU on its own engine counters (Sep 30 13:29–13:34). The engines count {ec_req}× the requests and about {ec_ppr}× the prompt tokens per request that the request logs record, so about {ec_hub_ratio}× the tokens in total, for reasons not yet established. The {hub_avg} M in older notes is the whole hub's average per GPU over the same 15 minutes.
Production on the same requests is scored minute by minute with the same rule, from its own request logs. {prod_rule_note}

one setting or code change, tested on top of the adopted settings at one load.

Adopted = in the adopted settings now. Rejected = tried and dropped; the reason is in the row. Baseline = a reference run with nothing changed. Invalid = the run broke and its result does not count. Finding = an analysis, kernel test or quality test with no SLA run. SIM = a simulation.
the share of GPU memory kept for processed prompts. More of it means fewer conversations get evicted and processed again.
each of our 4 engines uses 2 GPUs whose attention halves step together, so a long prompt on one pauses generation on both. Production's layout avoids this.
our gateway keeps each conversation on the same GPU pair so its cache is reused, and sends new conversations to the least-busy pair.
the cache-aware router production uses. On our layout it lost cache hits ({hit:dyn_05x}–{hit:dyn2_05x} vs our gateway's {hit:v3_tpc_05x}), so we route with our own gateway.
our speculative decoding: a small draft model proposes 7 tokens and the main model checks them in one step. Production uses a different draft (DFlash2) with block 4.

sessions_per_node.headline: The number to track is active sessions per node per minute. A production node at peak has 205 (430 requests per minute). Off-peak, it has 130 (275 requests per minute). Our node passes the SLA at 165 (325 requests per minute). This is 80% of a production node at peak.
sessions_per_node.defs: Session = distinct prompt_cache_key. Active per minute = sessions with at least one request starting that minute. In flight = sessions with a request open at that moment (sampled every 10 s; production timing for production rows, ours for ours). Production rows: every logged request of both load balancers, divided by 24 nodes (cross-checked against one node's session-hash share: 1,582 vs 1,559 sessions per 15 min, 213 vs 209 per minute).

sessions_per_node.caveat: Peak and off-peak hours from the log volume curve: Sep 30 13:00 PDT is the day's peak (equal to Oct 1's 21:00 PDT peak); the lowest hour seen (Oct 1 16:00 PDT) has 0.47× the peak volume, so the deepest off-peak may be nearer 100 active sessions per minute. The logs undercount production by about 1.1× in requests.
